title: George Lewis's reputation and role in the hall
summary: Asked about George Lewis, Jaffe says he was one of the few names he knew before coming and was seen as the last pure musician in town.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Well, can we touch the subject side to the actual musical aspects of the hall and the people that you were, how you decided to go about choosing a particular band and particularly is to be used in a book about George Lewis. What sort of role do you feel that George played in the development of the hall and it's, you know, kind of working out? He was one of the, you know, few musicians whose name I knew before I came here. You know, the people, you know, involved with the punk band, you know, records I heard, of the Eureka Brass Band, of actual musicians' names. And then after we got to town, you know, and we'd talk to people about, you know, where can I get to hear music and stuff, most of them would always, you know, they would also, you know, talk about George Lewis as one, you know, named musician. Maya Shermer, you know, the woman whose work was Wisconsin, you know, and she knew, you know, because he went to Europe and things. And, you know, he had, he had the reputation then, you know, the same as that, like, the look story reputation, as being the last, you know, pure musician in town. The musicians himself, I think, you know, sort of thought of him as, you know, just another, you know, guy hustling for a job. I mean, even, you know, at that time. He was playing, you know, the first time, you know, we went to a session in the hall. And I remember, you know, Dick Allen, you know, saying, you know, that's George Lewis, you know, when he came in, you know, he pointed out.
Tom Decker, his human and Russell, came over for the first time.
